{{Short description|Theorem of group theory}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically [[group theory]], '''Frobenius's theorem''' states that if <math>n</math> [[divisor|divides]] the [[order of a group|order]] of a [[finite group|finite]] [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math>, then the number of solutions of <math>x^n=1</math> in <math>G</math> is a multiple of <math>n</math>. It was introduced by {{harvs|txt|last=Frobenius|year=1903|authorlink=Ferdinand Georg Frobenius}}.

== Statement ==

A more general version of Frobenius's theorem states that if <math>C</math> is a [[conjugacy class]] with <math>h</math> elements of a finite group <math>G</math> with <math>g</math> elements and <math>n</math> is a positive [[integer]], then the number of elements <math>k</math> such that <math>k^n</math> is in <math>C</math> is a multiple of the [[greatest common divisor]] <math>(hn,g)</math> {{harv|Hall|1959|loc=theorem 9.1.1}}.

== Applications ==

One application of Frobenius's theorem is to show that the coefficients of the [[Artin–Hasse exponential]] are <math>p</math>-integral, by interpreting them in terms of the number of elements of order a power of <math>p</math> in the [[symmetric group]] <math>S_n</math>.

== Frobenius's conjecture ==

Frobenius [[conjecture]]d that if, in addition, the number of solutions to <math>x^n=1</math> is exactly <math>n</math>, where <math>n</math> divides the order of <math>G</math>, then these solutions form a [[normal subgroup]]. This was [[mathematical proof|proved]] by Iiyori and Yamaki<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Iiyori |first=Nobuo |last2=Yamaki |first2=Hiroyoshi |date=October 1991 |title=On a conjecture of Frobenius |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1991-25-02/S0273-0979-1991-16084-2/S0273-0979-1991-16084-2.pdf |journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=413–416 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1991-16084-2}}</ref> as a consequence of the [[classification of finite simple groups]].

The symmetric group <math>S_3</math> has exactly <math>4</math> solutions to <math>x^4=1</math> but these do not form a normal subgroup; this is not a [[counterexample]] to the conjecture as <math>4</math> does not divide <math>|S_3| = 6</math>.
